unit.title: Prepare and produce cakes and puddings products

theory1.instructions: Answer all 45 questions. Each question has one best answer: choose it. Each question is worth 1 mark. Time allowed: 2 hours 30 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

questions.stem: Before you start making a cake, what should you do first?
options: Taste the raw cake mix to check the sugar
Put on your watch so you can time the bake
Wash your hands and cover your hair
Turn the oven to its highest setting

questions.stem: Which eggs should you use for a cake or pudding?
options: Clean eggs with no cracks, within date
Cracked eggs, as long as you bake them
Eggs left in the sun to warm them up
Any eggs at all, as the cake will be cooked anyway

questions.stem: Why is it unsafe to taste raw cake batter made with raw eggs and flour?
options: It will make the cake rise less in the oven
It will spoil the colour of the finished cake
It makes the sugar dissolve too quickly
Raw eggs and raw flour can carry harmful germs

questions.stem: Which allergens are in a plain sponge cake made with flour, butter, sugar and eggs?
options: Fish, shellfish and celery
Peanuts, sesame and lupin
Soya, mustard and sulphites
Gluten, milk and eggs

questions.stem: A customer asks if the rum cake has nuts in it. What should you do?
options: Say no, because rum cake is always made without nuts
Check the recipe and the labels, then tell them
Guess from how the cake looks on the plate
Tell them to eat a small piece to find out

questions.stem: Why should you read the whole recipe before you start?
options: So you can leave out the steps you do not like
So you have everything ready in time
So the oven heats up faster than normal
So you can make the cake without weighing

questions.stem: Why are cake ingredients weighed on scales, in grams, instead of measured in cups?
options: Scales make the flour lighter and finer
Cups are not allowed in a kitchen
Weighing means you can skip sifting the flour
Weighing is more accurate each time

questions.stem: How should a cake tin be prepared for a sponge cake?
options: Wet it with water so the cake slides out
Leave it dry, as cakes do not stick
Pour a layer of oil in the bottom
Grease it and line it with baking paper

questions.stem: Why do you preheat the oven before the cake goes in?
options: To dry out the tins before you fill them
To save power by cooking the cake faster
So the cake starts baking at the right heat
So the oven door can be left open during baking

questions.stem: A sponge recipe says to bake in a moderate oven. Which range is usual, as the recipe and oven maker say?
options: About 80–100 °C
About 170–190 °C
About 240–260 °C
About 300–320 °C

questions.stem: Compared with a sponge, how is a rich fruit cake, such as Jamaican black cake, usually baked?
options: At a lower heat for a much longer time
At a much higher heat for a shorter time
At the same heat for the same time
In a microwave on the highest power

questions.stem: What does baking powder do in a cake?
options: It makes the cake sweeter and darker
It gives off gas that makes the cake rise
It stops the cake from going stale for weeks
It holds the fat and water together

questions.stem: Bicarbonate of soda needs an acid to work. Which ingredient in a bulla or a gingerbread gives some acid?
options: White sugar
Molasses
Cornflour
Salt

questions.stem: Why is soft (cake) flour often used for sponges, rather than strong bread flour?
options: It has less protein, giving a soft crumb
It has more protein, so the cake is chewy
It has added yeast to help the cake rise
It needs no sifting before it is used

questions.stem: In a creamed cake, what do the eggs mainly do?
options: Add colour and nothing else
Make the cake taste salty
Trap air and set the cake
Stop the butter from melting

questions.stem: In the creaming method, which ingredients are beaten together first?
options: Flour and eggs
Flour and milk
Eggs and baking powder
Fat and sugar

questions.stem: How do you know the fat and sugar have been creamed enough?
options: The mix is dark brown and runny
The sugar has melted into a syrup
The mix has turned hard and lumpy
The mix is pale, light and fluffy

questions.stem: Why are the eggs added to the creamed mix a little at a time?
options: To stop the mix from curdling (separating)
To make the eggs cook before baking
To save time when the kitchen is busy
So that much less flour is needed later on

questions.stem: The cake mix needs scraping down from the sides of the mixer bowl. What should you do?
options: Scrape it with a spatula while it runs slowly
Use your fingers while the beater is turning
Switch off the mixer, then scrape the bowl
Lift the guard and scrape on high speed

questions.stem: How should the flour be added to a creamed or whisked mix?
options: Beat it in hard with the mixer on high
Pour it all in at once and stir it round fast
Sift it and fold it in gently with a spoon
Melt it in a pan first, then pour it in

questions.stem: Which of these is made by the rubbing-in method?
options: Whisked Swiss roll
Victoria sandwich
Rock cakes
Gingerbread

questions.stem: What should a rubbed-in mix of flour and fat look like before the liquid is added?
options: A smooth, shiny dough
Fine breadcrumbs
A runny batter
Large lumps of fat

questions.stem: For a whisked sponge, the eggs and sugar are whisked until a trail stays on top for a few seconds. What is this called?
options: The soft-ball stage
The rubbing-in stage
The ribbon stage
The setting point

questions.stem: Why must oven gloves be dry when you take a hot tin out of the oven?
options: Wet gloves are harder to wash afterwards
Dry gloves make the tin cool down faster
Heat passes through wet cloth quickly
Wet gloves leave marks on the cake top

questions.stem: Which method is used for gingerbread and bulla, where the sugar, molasses and fat are warmed together first?
options: The creaming method
The whisking method
The rubbing-in method
The melting method

questions.stem: Why are the dried fruits for a Jamaican black cake often soaked in rum and wine for days or weeks?
options: To make the fruit lighter so it floats on top
To soften the fruit and give a rich flavour
To remove all the sugar from the fruit
To keep the fruit from burning in the oven

questions.stem: Dried fruit has sunk to the bottom of a fruit cake. What is a likely cause?
options: The cake was cooled on a wire rack
The tin was greased and lined with paper first
The mix was too soft or the fruit was wet
The eggs were added a little at a time

questions.stem: Why should you not open the oven door during the first part of baking a sponge?
options: The oven light may break with the cold air
Cold air can make the cake sink
The cake will turn a darker colour
The baking paper may catch fire

questions.stem: How can you test whether a sponge cake is baked?
options: It wobbles in the middle when shaken
It springs back when pressed lightly
It sticks to your finger when touched
It is still pale on top and sides

questions.stem: You push a clean skewer into the middle of a fruit cake. What shows it is baked?
options: It comes out clean
It comes out wet with mix
It will not go into the cake
It comes out hot and sticky

questions.stem: A cake has risen to a peak and cracked on top. What is a likely cause?
options: The oven was too cool
The oven was set too hot
The tin was too large
Too little flour was used

questions.stem: A cake has sunk in the middle. Which is a likely cause?
options: The tin was greased and lined well
The flour was sifted twice
The cake was left to cool in the tin for 5 minutes
Too much raising agent, or it was underbaked

questions.stem: A cake has a heavy, close texture. Which is a likely cause?
options: The fat and sugar were creamed until fluffy
The oven was preheated
The mix was not creamed enough
The cake was cooled on a wire rack

questions.stem: How should most cakes be cooled after baking?
options: Put in the fridge while still very hot
A few minutes in the tin, then on a wire rack
Left in the tin overnight in the oven
Wrapped in cling film straight from the oven

questions.stem: Why must a cake be fully cool before it is iced with buttercream?
options: Or the buttercream will melt and slide off
So the cake becomes hard and dry
So the icing sugar dissolves into it
Because a warm cake cannot be cut into slices

questions.stem: Which icing sets hard and is often used on Jamaican wedding and Christmas fruit cakes?
options: Royal icing
Whipped cream
Glacé icing
Fresh custard

questions.stem: A rum cake is often soaked with a rum syrup after baking. When is the syrup usually added?
options: Before the mix goes into the tin
Only after the cake is a week old
While the cake is still warm
Just before it is served, on the plate

questions.stem: When steaming a pudding in a basin, why is a pleat folded into the paper and foil cover?
options: To let the steam pour into the pudding
To make the pudding easier to turn out
To stop the basin from cracking in the heat
To leave space so the pudding can rise

questions.stem: What should you check often while a pudding is steaming?
options: That the pudding has not changed colour
That the kitchen door is kept closed
That the cover has been taken off
That the water has not boiled away

questions.stem: How should you lift the lid off a steamer?
options: Tilt it away from you so steam goes the other way
Lift it straight up towards your face
Pull it towards you quickly to save time
Use a wet cloth to hold the hot handle

questions.stem: How is a Jamaican sweet potato pudding usually cooked?
options: Steamed in a covered basin for four hours
Deep-fried in hot oil until crisp
Set in the fridge with gelatine and no cooking
Baked in the oven until set and golden

questions.stem: Why must an egg custard sauce never be allowed to boil?
options: The eggs will scramble and the sauce curdles
The milk will turn into cream
The sauce will become too thin to pour
The vanilla will lose all its colour

questions.stem: Why are baked egg custards often cooked in a tray of hot water (a bain-marie)?
options: To cook them gently so they do not curdle
To stop them from rising too high
To make them cook in half the time
To clean the dishes at the same time as they bake

questions.stem: A cake is filled with fresh cream. How should it be stored, or as the Centre's food safety plan says?
options: In the fridge at 5 °C or below
On the counter in a warm kitchen
In a sunny window to keep it soft
In the oven with the heat turned off

questions.stem: Why are cakes and puddings labelled with their name and date when they are stored?
options: So staff know who baked the best cake
So the newest cakes are sold first
So the price can be changed each day
So stock is used in date order, first in, first out

theory2.instructions: Section A has 15 short answers (2 marks each). Section B has 10 essay questions (5 marks each): answer each in full sentences. Time allowed: 3 hours 35 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

shortAnswers.stem: What permit must every food handler in Jamaica hold, from the local health department?
What is the range of temperatures between about 5 °C and 63 °C, in which germs grow fast, called?
Which tool is used to sift flour, to take out lumps and add air?
What flexible rubber or silicone tool is used to scrape a mixing bowl clean?
What type of flour has a raising agent already mixed into it?
A Victoria sandwich uses equal weights of flour, fat, sugar and eggs. If you use 200 g of flour, how many grams of butter do you need?
Which spice, called "pimento" in Jamaica, is often used in puddings and fruit cakes?
What is the dark burnt-sugar colouring often added to Jamaican fruit cake called?
What is the name of the small, square Jamaican coconut cake, spiced with nutmeg and often sold in school tuck shops?
What is the name of the flat, round Jamaican cake made with molasses or wet sugar and ginger, often eaten with cheese or pear?
Besides sweet potato, which yellow ground grain is used to make a popular Jamaican baked pudding with coconut milk?
Marzipan (almond paste) is often put under the icing on fruit cakes. Which allergen does it contain?
What is the pudding called that is made by layering buttered bread with dried fruit and baking it in an egg custard?
What is one serving of cake, cut to a set size so every customer gets the same amount, called?
What tool with a long, flat, bendy blade is used to spread icing smoothly on a cake?

essays.stem: Describe the personal hygiene and food safety steps you follow when making cakes and puddings.
essays.modelAnswer: I hold a Food Handler's Permit from the local health department. I come to work clean, in a clean uniform and apron, with my hair covered, nails short and no jewellery except a plain band if the Centre allows it. I wash my hands well before I start, after handling raw eggs, after touching my face or the bin, and after using the toilet. I report to my supervisor if I am ill. I use clean, uncracked eggs within their date and keep eggs, milk, butter and cream cold, at 5 °C or below, or as the Centre's food safety plan says. I do not taste raw batter. I keep raw ingredients away from finished cakes and use clean tools. I know the allergens in each recipe and label them. I cool, cover, label and date the finished products and use them in date order.
markingPoints: Food Handler's Permit; clean uniform, hair covered, no jewellery, reports illness
Washes hands at the right times
Uses clean, uncracked eggs and keeps dairy cold (5 °C or below, or as the plan says)
Does not taste raw batter; keeps raw and finished items apart with clean tools
Knows and labels allergens; cools, covers, labels, dates and rotates stock

essays.stem: Describe how you prepare (your mise en place) before you start making a batch of cakes.
essays.modelAnswer: "Mise en place" means having everything in its place before I start. I read the whole recipe and check how many cakes are needed. I check that I have all the ingredients, that they are within date, and I note the allergens. I collect the equipment I need: scales, bowls, sieve, mixer, spatula, tins, baking paper and a wire rack, and I check the mixer guard and plug are in good order. I weigh every ingredient accurately in grams. I take the butter and eggs out of the fridge a short time before, so they cream well, as the recipe says. I grease and line the tins. I set the oven shelves in the middle and preheat the oven to the temperature the recipe and oven maker say. I keep my work area clean and tidy as I go.
markingPoints: Reads the recipe and checks quantities
Checks ingredients, dates and allergens
Collects and checks equipment, including the mixer guard
Weighs ingredients accurately and prepares the butter and eggs
Greases and lines tins and preheats the oven; keeps the area clean

essays.stem: Describe, step by step, how to make a Victoria sandwich by the creaming method.
essays.modelAnswer: I preheat the oven to a moderate heat, about 170–190 °C or as the recipe and oven maker say, and grease and line two sandwich tins. I weigh equal amounts of soft butter, caster sugar, self-raising flour and eggs. I beat the butter and sugar together until the mix is pale, light and fluffy, which traps air. I beat the eggs and add them a little at a time, beating well after each addition so the mix does not curdle; if it starts to curdle, I add a spoonful of the flour. I sift the flour and fold it in gently with a metal spoon or spatula, so I do not knock the air out. I share the mix equally between the tins and level the tops. I bake until golden and springy, then cool on a wire rack before filling with jam and buttercream.
markingPoints: Preheats oven to a moderate heat and prepares tins
Weighs equal amounts of the four main ingredients
Creams butter and sugar until pale and fluffy
Adds eggs gradually and folds in sifted flour gently
Divides evenly, bakes until springy, cools on a rack, then fills

essays.stem: Explain the job of each main ingredient in a cake: flour, sugar, fat, eggs and raising agent.
essays.modelAnswer: Flour gives the cake its structure, the framework that holds it up. Soft flour, with less protein, is used for a light, tender crumb. Sugar gives sweetness and colour to the crust, keeps the cake moist and helps trap air when it is creamed with the fat. Fat, such as butter or margarine, makes the cake tender and moist, adds flavour and, when creamed, holds tiny air bubbles. Eggs trap air when beaten, help hold the fat and liquid together, and set when heated, which helps give the cake its shape. They also add colour and flavour. The raising agent, such as baking powder, gives off carbon dioxide gas when it is wet and heated, which makes the cake rise. Bicarbonate of soda needs an acid, such as molasses or buttermilk, to work.
markingPoints: Flour gives structure; soft flour gives a tender crumb
Sugar gives sweetness, colour and moisture and helps trap air
Fat gives tenderness, flavour and holds air when creamed
Eggs trap air, bind and set to give shape
Raising agent gives off gas to make it rise; bicarbonate needs an acid

essays.stem: Compare the creaming method and the whisking method. Say how each puts air into the cake, and give an example of each.
essays.modelAnswer: In the creaming method, fat and sugar are beaten together until pale and fluffy. The sharp sugar crystals cut tiny air pockets into the fat. Eggs are then beaten in a little at a time and the flour is folded in. The raising agent in the flour adds more lift. Creamed cakes, such as a Victoria sandwich or a butter cake, are rich, moist and keep well. In the whisking method, eggs and sugar are whisked together, usually with little or no fat, until the mix is thick and pale and reaches the ribbon stage. The air is trapped in the egg foam, and the flour is folded in very gently so the air is not lost. Whisked sponges, such as a Swiss roll or a sponge for trifle, are very light but dry out more quickly.
markingPoints: Creaming: fat and sugar beaten until fluffy, air trapped in the fat
Example of a creamed cake (for example, Victoria sandwich)
Whisking: eggs and sugar whisked to the ribbon stage, air trapped in the egg foam
Example of a whisked cake (for example, Swiss roll)
Compares the results: creamed richer and keeps longer; whisked lighter, dries sooner

essays.stem: Describe three common faults in cakes, the likely cause of each, and how to prevent them.
essays.modelAnswer: A cake that sinks in the middle may have had too much raising agent, the oven door may have been opened too early, or it may have been taken out before it was baked. To prevent this, I weigh the raising agent carefully, keep the door shut in the first part of baking and test the cake before taking it out. A cake that peaks and cracks on top was usually baked in an oven that was too hot, or on a shelf too high. I check the oven temperature and use the middle shelf. A cake with a heavy, close texture may not have been creamed enough, the eggs may have curdled, or the flour was beaten in too hard. I cream until pale and fluffy, add the eggs slowly and fold the flour in gently. Fruit that sinks means the mix was too soft or the fruit was wet.
markingPoints: Names a first fault with a correct cause
Gives a correct way to prevent the first fault
Names a second fault with a correct cause and prevention
Names a third fault with a correct cause and prevention
Uses correct terms (creaming, curdling, folding, oven heat)

essays.stem: Describe how to steam a sponge pudding safely, from preparing the basin to turning it out.
essays.modelAnswer: I grease the pudding basin well and put a little jam or syrup in the bottom if the recipe says. I make the sponge mix by the creaming method and fill the basin about two-thirds full, so the pudding has room to rise. I cover it with greaseproof paper and foil with a pleat folded in the middle, and tie it on firmly with string, making a string handle to lift it. I place it in a steamer, or on a trivet in a large pan with boiling water about halfway up the basin, and put the lid on. I steam it for the time the recipe says, checking often that the water has not boiled away and topping up with boiling water. I lift the lid away from me to avoid steam burns and use dry oven gloves. When it is cooked and springy, I loosen the edges and turn it out onto a warm plate.
markingPoints: Greases the basin and fills about two-thirds full
Covers with paper and foil with a pleat and ties it firmly
Steams with boiling water at the right level for the recipe time
Checks the water often and tops up with boiling water
Lifts lids away from the face, uses dry gloves and turns out when cooked

essays.stem: Describe how to make and bake a Jamaican sweet potato pudding, and how you know it is cooked.
essays.modelAnswer: I wash and peel the sweet potatoes, then grate them finely, keeping my fingers clear of the grater and using a guard or holding the last piece with care. I mix the grated potato with a little flour or cornmeal, brown sugar, coconut milk, melted butter, vanilla, grated nutmeg, cinnamon and a pinch of salt, and add raisins if the recipe uses them. The mix should be like a thick batter. I pour it into a greased baking tin and bake it in a moderate oven, about 160–180 °C or as the recipe and oven maker say, for the time the recipe gives, often more than an hour. The pudding is cooked when it is set and firm, the top is golden with a soft custard-like layer, and a skewer in the middle comes out clean. I cool it, then cut it into even portions. I label the allergens, such as milk and wheat.
markingPoints: Prepares and grates the sweet potato safely
Mixes with suitable ingredients (coconut milk, sugar, spices, flour or cornmeal)
Bakes in a greased tin at a moderate heat as the recipe and oven maker say
Knows it is cooked: set, firm, golden, skewer comes out clean
Cools, portions evenly and labels the allergens

essays.stem: Explain how to finish, portion and present a cake for sale in a café or hotel.
essays.modelAnswer: I make sure the cake is completely cool before I finish it, or the icing will melt. I trim the top level if needed and brush off loose crumbs. I may fill it with jam and buttercream, cover it with a thin crumb coat, chill it, then put on the final coat and smooth it with a palette knife. I may decorate it with piping, fresh fruit, toasted coconut or a dusting of icing sugar, keeping it neat and simple. I mark the cake into even portions so every customer gets the same amount and the cost is controlled, then cut with a clean, hot, dry knife, wiping it between cuts. I present it on a clean cake board or stand, with a label showing its name, price and allergens. Cream cakes are displayed in a chiller at 5 °C or below, or as the Centre's food safety plan says.
markingPoints: Finishes only when fully cool; trims and removes crumbs
Fills and coats neatly using a palette knife
Decorates neatly and simply
Marks and cuts even portions with a clean, hot knife for cost control
Presents cleanly with a label (name, price, allergens), chilling cream cakes

essays.stem: Explain how cakes and puddings should be cooled, stored and labelled to keep them safe and fresh.
essays.modelAnswer: After baking, I leave most cakes in the tin for a few minutes, then turn them out onto a wire rack so the steam escapes and the bottom does not go soggy. Puddings and custards that will be served cold are cooled quickly, then covered and put in the fridge. Plain sponges, fruit cakes, toto and bulla are stored in clean, airtight containers in a cool, dry place, away from strong smells and pests. Fruit cakes soaked in rum keep for a long time if wrapped well. Anything with fresh cream, custard or other dairy fillings, and cut puddings, are kept covered in the fridge at 5 °C or below, or as the Centre's food safety plan says. Every container is labelled with the product name, the date made, a use-by date and the allergens. Stock is used first in, first out.
markingPoints: Cools cakes on a wire rack and cools puddings quickly
Stores plain and fruit cakes airtight in a cool, dry place
Keeps cream, custard and dairy items covered in the fridge at 5 °C or below (or as the plan says)
Labels with name, dates and allergens
Uses stock first in, first out

practical1.title: Make creamed cupcakes and a tray of Jamaican toto, then finish and present them
practical1.brief: Work in the Centre's training kitchen, in clean uniform with hair covered. As a group, read the recipes, list the allergens and set up the work area. Each member makes their own batch of 6 cupcakes by the creaming method: weigh the ingredients, line the tray, cream the butter and sugar until pale and fluffy, add the egg a little at a time, fold in the sifted flour and bake at the heat the recipe and oven maker say. Then the group makes one tray of toto (coconut cake) together, with each member doing a named stage: weighing, grating or preparing the coconut, mixing, filling and levelling the tray, and testing when baked. When the cupcakes are cool, each member pipes or spreads buttercream on their own batch. The group cuts the toto into even portions, labels everything with the name, date and allergens, and cleans down. Photograph each stage below and add the photos to the group's practical. Hand in once for the whole group.
materials: Butter or margarine, caster sugar, self-raising flour, eggs, milk and vanilla for the cupcakes
Grated or desiccated coconut, flour, brown sugar, butter, baking powder, nutmeg and other spices for the toto
Icing sugar and butter for buttercream
Scales, bowls, sieves, wooden spoons, spatulas, a mixer with its guard, piping bags and palette knives
Cupcake trays and paper cases, a baking tray or tin, baking paper and a wire rack
Oven, dry oven gloves, labels and pens, and cleaning materials
photos: The group in clean uniform, hair covered, with the work area set up
Ingredients weighed out for one member's cupcakes
Creamed butter and sugar, pale and fluffy
Cupcake cases filled evenly and ready for the oven
The toto mix spread level in its tray
Baked cupcakes and toto cooling on a wire rack
Finished cupcakes with buttercream, and the toto cut into even portions
Products labelled with name, date and allergens, and the clean work area
checklist: Washed hands, wore clean uniform with hair covered and no jewellery
Weighed all ingredients accurately in grams
Creamed the fat and sugar until pale and fluffy and added the egg gradually without curdling
Folded in the sifted flour gently and filled the cases evenly
Used the oven safely with dry oven gloves and baked at the correct heat
Tested correctly when baked and cooled the products on a wire rack
Finished the cupcakes neatly and cut the toto into even portions
Labelled with name, date and allergens and cleaned the work area and equipment
safety: Keep the mixer guard in place and switch the mixer off before scraping the bowl
Use dry oven gloves for hot trays and tell others when you are carrying something hot
Use a grater with care and keep fingers clear of the blade
Wipe up spills at once so nobody slips
Use clean, uncracked eggs and do not taste raw mix

practical2.title: Make whisked Swiss rolls and a Jamaican sweet potato pudding
practical2.brief: Work in the Centre's training kitchen, in clean uniform with hair covered. As a group, read the recipes, list the allergens and set up. The group makes one sweet potato pudding together and puts it in the oven first, because it bakes for longer: each member does a named stage (peeling, grating, mixing in the coconut milk, sugar and spices, greasing the tin and filling it). While it bakes, each member makes their own small Swiss roll by the whisking method: line the tray, whisk the eggs and sugar to the ribbon stage, fold in the sifted flour gently, spread the mix evenly, bake, turn out onto sugared paper, spread with jam and roll it up neatly. Each member checks the pudding once with a skewer at the end of baking, with the assessor watching. Then the group cools and cuts the pudding into even portions, labels everything with the name, date and allergens, and cleans down. Photograph each stage below and add the photos to the group's practical. Hand in once for the whole group.
materials: Sweet potatoes, coconut milk, brown sugar, flour or cornmeal, butter, vanilla, nutmeg, cinnamon, salt and raisins
Eggs, caster sugar, soft flour and jam for the Swiss rolls
Scales, bowls, a hand or electric whisk, sieves, spatulas, a grater, peelers and palette knives
Swiss roll trays, a deep baking tin, baking paper, a skewer and a wire rack
Oven, dry oven gloves, labels and pens, and cleaning materials
photos: The group in clean uniform with the work area set up and allergens listed
Sweet potato being grated safely and the pudding mix in the tin
Eggs and sugar whisked to the ribbon stage
Swiss roll mix spread evenly in the lined tray
A Swiss roll being rolled up on sugared paper
The skewer test on the baked pudding
Finished Swiss rolls sliced and the pudding cut into even portions
Products labelled with name, date and allergens, and the clean work area
checklist: Washed hands, wore clean uniform with hair covered and no jewellery
Prepared and grated the sweet potato safely and took part in mixing the pudding
Whisked the eggs and sugar to the ribbon stage
Folded in the flour gently without losing the air
Spread the mix evenly, baked it correctly and rolled it without large cracks
Tested the pudding correctly with a skewer and judged when it was cooked
Cut even portions and labelled with name, date and allergens
Used the oven safely with dry gloves and cleaned the area and equipment
safety: Keep fingers clear of the grater and peeler; do not grate the last small piece
Use dry oven gloves and keep the deep pudding tin level when carrying it
Switch off and unplug an electric whisk before removing the beaters
Wipe up spills at once so nobody slips
Cool the pudding, then cover and chill it at 5 °C or below, or as the Centre's food safety plan says
